stemBlocks.value: A car costing $1 500 000 depreciates by 15% per year. Calculate its value after 2 years.
Think first: Depreciation is compound: the second year of 15% is taken off the already reduced value, not off the original price.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p020-q19 from workbook page 20.

solutionSteps.instruction: Apply it for the first year.
Apply it again for the second year.

strategyBlocks.value: Use the multiplier 0.85 once for each year, so multiply $1 500 000 by 0.85 squared.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: After 2 years the car is worth $1 083 750.

whyThisWorks.value: Each year the car loses 15% of whatever it is worth at the start of that year, so the base shrinks annually. The total loss over two years is 27.75%, not 30%, because the second year of loss comes from a smaller amount. Repeated multiplication by the same multiplier is exactly what raising it to a power means.

commonErrors.misconception: Taking 30% off in one go and getting $1 050 000.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Taking 30% off in one go and getting $1 050 000.

commonErrors.misconception: Subtracting $225 000 twice, treating the depreciation as simple rather than compound.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Subtracting $225 000 twice, treating the depreciation as simple rather than compound.

examTip.value: For any repeated percentage change, find the one-step multiplier first and raise it to the power of the number of steps. It works for growth and decay alike.
